body.text: Why does Michael D. Bordo still shape capital allocation and market pricing across global desks? Behind the headline numbers lies a structural mechanism that quietly governs liquidity, risk, and long-term purchasing power.

Michael David Bordo (born 1942) is a Canadian-American economist and economic historian whose research focuses on monetary history, international monetary economics, monetary policy, monetary economics, financial stability (especially financial crises), central banking, and international monetary arrangements.

He is an emeritus Board of Governors Professor of Economics and an emeritus Distinguished Professor of Economics at Rutgers University, where he formerly directed the Center for Monetary and Financial History.

He is a research associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), a distinguished visitor at the Griswold Center for Economic Policy Studies at Princeton University, and the Duncan Stewart Distinguished Visiting Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University.

body.text: Bordo's research examines the historical performance of monetary institutions and policy regimes, particularly the classical gold standard and the interwar gold exchange standard, the Bretton Woods system, and the evolution of the Federal Reserve and other central banks. He has also focused on two eras of upheaval: the Great Depression and the Great Inflation.

His scholarship has addressed the relationship between monetary credibility, price level and real economic stability, and financial stability, the historical causes and consequences of financial crises, and the development of international financial integration. He has collaborated extensively with economists including Anna J.

Schwartz, Barry Eichengreen, Hugh Rockoff, Ehsan Choudhri, Ronald MacDonald, Robert McCauley, Eric Monnet, Marc Flandreau, Catherine Schenk, Lars Jonung, Joseph G. Haubrich, Eugene White, David Wheelock, John Landon-Lane, Angela Redish, Harold James, and others.

According to the September 2026 RePEc/IDEAS rankings, Bordo ranked fifth among 1,978 researchers classified in business, economic, and financial history. As of October 31, 2026, his research had received 7,601 citations in the RePEc CitEc database, with an h-index of 46.
com reports 29,593 citations to Bordo's publications and a discipline-specific h-index (D-index) of 86 in economics and finance. Google Scholar estimates 36,685 citations.

Bordo served as president of the Economic History Association from 2016 to 2017 and has been a member of the Shadow Open Market Committee since 2009. He has authored or edited numerous books on monetary economics, central banking, and economic history.
His collected research is housed in the archives of the Hoover Institution at Stanford University.
Education

Bordo was born in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, in 1942. He received his Bachelor of Arts degree in economics and political science from McGill University in 1963 and a Master of Science degree in economics from the London School of Economics in 1965.
Career and contribution

Bordo began his academic career at Carleton University in Ottawa, Canada, where he served as an assistant professor and subsequently an associate professor of economics from 1969 to 1981. He joined the University of South Carolina as a professor of economics in 1981 and remained there until 1989, when he moved to Rutgers University.

At Rutgers, Bordo became a Distinguished Professor of Economics in 1993 and served as director of the Center for Monetary and Financial History beginning in 1990. He later held the Board of Governors Professorship of Economics. In 2025, he became an emeritus professor at Rutgers.

Throughout his career, Bordo has held visiting academic appointments at universities including Harvard University, Princeton University, the University of Cambridge, the London School of Economics, Carnegie Mellon University, the University of California, Los Angeles, and the Paris School of Economics.

At Cambridge, he served as Pitt Professor of American History and Institutions during the 2006, 2007 academic year and was a fellow of King's College, Cambridge. He has also held a number of visiting research fellowships at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University.

Bordo has held visiting and research appointments at central banks and international monetary institutions, including the International Monetary Fund, the Bank for International Settlements, the Bank of Canada, the Bank of England, the Bank of France, the Bank of Italy, the Sveriges Riksbank, the Czech National Bank, the Swiss National Bank, the Norges Bank, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and several regional Federal Reserve Banks, including the Federal Reserve Banks of St.
He has maintained a longstanding affiliation with the National Bureau of Economic Research, where he has served as a research associate in monetary economics and economic history.

His academic research has appeared in many leading journals, including the American Economic Review,Journal of International Economics, Journal of Political Economy,Journal of Money, Credit and Banking, Journal of Monetary Economics, The Journal of Economic History, and Journal of International Money and Finance.
Research and contributions

Bordo's research combines economic history with monetary theory and empirical macroeconomics. Much of his work uses historical evidence to evaluate the performance of monetary arrangements and the role of central banks in maintaining price stability, financial stability, and international monetary cooperation.

His research extends from the classical gold standard of the nineteenth century to contemporary debates over monetary-policy rules, financial crises, asset price booms and busts, and digital currencies.
The quantity of money and the economy

Bordo's earliest research was conducted within the modern quantity theory of money framework developed by Milton Friedman, under whom he completed his doctoral dissertation at the University of Chicago.
Friedman's 1956 restatement of the quantity theory emphasized the stability of the demand for money and the relationship between changes in the money supply and economic activity.

In his dissertation research, published as "The Income Effects of the Sources of Monetary Change: An Historical Approach" in Economic Inquiry in 1975, Bordo investigated whether the economic effects of monetary change depended on how additional money entered the economy, such as through gold discoveries, changes in bank lending, or monetary operations by central banks.

Using historical evidence from different monetary arrangements in the United States between 1834 and 1914, he tested whether the sources of monetary change significantly affected the relationship between money and income.

He found that, in most of the cases examined, the source of monetary change had no significant independent effect on income, supporting the view that changes in the quantity of money were generally more important than the particular channels through which they originated.

Bordo extended this investigation to British monetary history in "The Income Effects of the Sources of New Money: A Comparison of the United States and the United Kingdom, 1870, 1913," published in Explorations in Economic History in 1977.

The article compared the relationship between sources of monetary expansion and economic activity in the United States and the United Kingdom during the classical gold standard era, extending the earlier American analysis into an international historical comparison.

Together, the two studies examined a central question in the debate between monetarist and Keynesian approaches to monetary economics: whether changes in the money supply affected economic activity primarily through their aggregate magnitude or whether their particular sources also mattered.
Bordo's subsequent research examined the transmission of monetary disturbances to relative prices and economic activity.

In "The Effects of Monetary Change on Relative Commodity Prices and the Role of Long-Term Contracts," published in the Journal of Political Economy in 1980, he investigated why prices in different industries respond at different speeds to changes in the money supply.

The paper developed an explanation based on differences in price flexibility across industries, emphasizing the role of implicit long-term contracts in determining the speed of price adjustment. data, Bordo found empirical support for the relationship between contract duration and the response of relative prices to monetary disturbances.
The study contributed to research on the transmission of monetary shocks and the role of price rigidities in the economy.
Bordo also studied the long-run behavior of the velocity of money, or the rate at which money circulates through an economy (the inverse of money demand).

In research with Lars Jonung, including their 1987 Cambridge University Press book The Long-Run Behavior of the Velocity of Circulation: The International Evidence, the authors examined historical patterns in money velocity across countries over more than a century.

They identified a long-run U-shaped pattern in which velocity initially declined as economies became increasingly monetized, stabilized, and subsequently rose with the development of more sophisticated financial institutions and payment arrangements.
